questions.q: A 2-month-old neonate is found to have a speckled lentiginous nevus with an associated port-wine stain and nevus anemicus on examination. The cutaneous lesions consist of a light-brown background with dark macular speckles in a polka-dot pattern. What is the underlying genetic driver of the naevus spilus component, and what is the syndromic diagnosis?
opts: TP53 mutation; Phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica
HRAS postzygotic somatic mutation; Phakomatosis spilorosea
PTEN mutation; Phakomatosis pigmentovascularis type IIa
NF1 mutation; Neurofibromatosis type 1 with nevus spilus features
questions.exp: Naevus spilus is driven by postzygotic somatic activating mutations in the HRAS gene (classically c.37G→C, p.Gly13Arg). The macular variant with an associated nevus flammeus and nevus anemicus is the hallmark cutaneous finding of Phakomatosis spilorosea (historically Phakomatosis pigmentovascularis type IIIb).
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: HRAS GENE (mustachioed KING) sits on the EMBRYOLOGICAL THRONE making SOMATIC MUTATIONS—when he wears his PORT-WINE CLOAK, it's PHAKOMATOSIS SPILOROSEA appearing in the castle!

questions.q: A 6-month-old girl is found to have a 55 cm lesion covering her entire left lower extremity with dozens of satellite nevi. Imaging shows involvement extending into the subcutaneous fat and underlying muscle. What is the most significant clinical concern regarding melanoma risk in this presentation?
opts: Melanoma arises exclusively at the dermal-epidermal junction, allowing early visual detection
Melanoma typically develops only in the epidermis, making dermoscopy highly sensitive
Melanoma may arise deep in the dermis or subcutis, rendering early visual detection difficult
Melanoma risk is negligible because the lesion is present at birth
questions.exp: Giant congenital melanocytic nevi (>40 cm) carry a substantial lifetime melanoma risk of 2–14%, and critically, melanoma may arise deep within the dermis or subcutis rather than at the epidermal surface. This deep origin makes clinical and dermoscopic detection challenging and emphasizes the need for imaging and close surveillance.

questions.q: A genetic counselor is explaining Cockayne Syndrome pathophysiology to parents of an affected child. Which of the following CORRECTLY identifies the primary molecular defect and the specific DNA repair pathway involved in Cockayne Syndrome?
opts: Defective nucleotide excision repair (NER) with inability to remove thymine dimers from any DNA region
Defective transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair (TC-NER) with inability to remove UV-induced photoproducts from actively transcribing genes
Defective mismatch repair (MMR) leading to accumulation of point mutations during DNA replication
Defective base excision repair (BER) with impaired recognition of oxidative DNA damage
questions.exp: Cockayne Syndrome is fundamentally driven by a defect in transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair (TC-NER), the specific sub-pathway responsible for removing UV-induced photoproducts and transcription-blocking lesions from actively transcribing genes. The pathognomonic molecular finding is the inability to recover mRNA synthesis after UV radiation exposure, resulting from autosomal recessive mutations in ERCC6 (80% of cases) or ERCC8 (20% of cases).

questions.q: A 9-year-old girl is diagnosed with tinea capitis presenting with diffuse scaling and polygonal-shaped areas of alopecia with finger-like margins. Multiple black dots are visible on the scalp, and Wood's lamp examination shows no fluorescence. What is the primary pathogenic mechanism that creates the characteristic 'black dot' appearance?
opts: Melanin oxidation from fungal production of tyrosinase
Accumulation of necrotic tissue debris at the hair follicle opening
Hair shaft breakage at the follicular ostium due to internal weakening by endophytic hyphae
External pigmented arthrospores coating the hair surface
questions.exp: In endothrix tinea capitis, hyphae penetrate and grow directly inside the hair shaft cortex, severely weakening it internally while the external cuticle remains intact. This internal damage causes the hair to break exactly at the level of the follicular ostium, leaving behind black dot remnants. This contrasts with ectothrix, where arthroconidia coat the external surface.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a TOWER (hair shaft) with a BOMB (endothrix fungus) planted INSIDE the walls—the tower collapses exactly at the GATEWAY (follicular ostium), leaving BLACK RUBBLE (black dots) at ground level, while the outer facade stays mysteriously intact.

questions.q: A 2-day-old term infant presents with a round, punched-out defect on the scalp vertex covered by a thin, translucent epithelial membrane. On careful examination, you note a ring of dark, coarse, radially oriented hair surrounding the lesion. Which of the following best explains the significance of this 'hair collar sign'?
opts: It indicates autosomal recessive inheritance and poor prognosis
It is a pathognomonic clinical marker for an underlying neural tube defect and warrants neuroimaging
It confirms the diagnosis is Adams-Oliver syndrome with limb defects
It demonstrates active immune-mediated destruction of hair follicles
questions.exp: The 'hair collar sign'—a ring of dark, coarse, radially oriented hair surrounding aplasia cutis congenita—is a pathognomonic feature of membranous ACC that serves as a clinical marker for underlying neural tube defects, necessitating neuroimaging evaluation. Aplasia cutis congenita is a structural developmental anomaly, not an autoimmune or immune-mediated process, and the hair collar sign is not specific to Adams-Oliver syndrome.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a KNIGHT'S COLLAR of dark, bristling HAIR encircling the crown of a castle tower—this COLLAR CROWN marks the SECRET TUNNEL (neural tube defect) beneath the stones.

questions.q: A 9-month-old with known Netherton syndrome previously presenting with neonatal erythroderma now develops migratory, polycyclic erythematous plaques with a distinctive serpiginous border featuring a characteristic 'double-edged scale.' Which phenotypic variant of Netherton syndrome is this clinical presentation most consistent with?
opts: Continuous skin peeling variant
Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (CIE)
Ichthyosis linearis circumflexa (ILC)
Bullous pemphigoid-like variant
questions.exp: Ichthyosis linearis circumflexa (ILC) is the characteristic mid-to-late infantile phenotypic variant that typically emerges as severe erythroderma subsides. It presents with pathognomonic migratory, serpiginous plaques bordered by a distinctive double-edged scale, representing the classic evolutionary progression of Netherton syndrome. The ILC variant is highly distinctive and considered pathognomonic for the condition.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a DOUBLE-EDGED SWORD (double-edged scale) slicing SERPENTINE PATHS (serpiginous plaques) through an ICY LANDSCAPE (ILC)—the plaques CIRCLE and MIGRATE like a knight's winding castle tour as the erythroderma FADES INTO HISTORY.

questions.q: Histopathological examination of a vitiliginous lesion in an 8-year-old reveals a complete absence of melanocytes in the basal layer with sparse CD8+ lymphocytic infiltration at the dermoepidermal junction. Which of the following melanocyte-specific markers would fail to stain in this lesional skin?
opts: Tyrosinase, TYRP1, DCT, MCHR1, and SOX10 (all target autoantigens)
Melan-A (MART-1), HMB-45, MITF, and DOPA stains
Keratins K5 and K14 (basal layer epidermal markers)
CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell markers only
questions.exp: Vitiligo is characterized by complete absence of melanocytes in the basal layer, which is confirmed by lack of staining with melanocyte-specific immunohistochemical markers including Melan-A (MART-1), HMB-45, MITF, and DOPA. Although tyrosinase, TYRP1, DCT, MCHR1, and SOX10 are the specific target autoantigens driving the CD8+ immune attack, the absence of melanocytes means these antigens are simply not present to be marked.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a rapidly enlarging, bright red pedunculated nodule on his finger that has been bleeding with minor trauma. On histology, lobular proliferations of capillary endothelial cells are seen in the superficial dermis within a fibromyxoid stroma, bounded by an epithelial collarette. According to the ISSVA classification, how should this lesion be categorized?
opts: Benign vascular malformation
Benign vascular tumour
Congenital vascular anomaly
Granulomatous infectious lesion
questions.exp: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary haemangioma) is officially classified by ISSVA as a benign vascular tumour, not a malformation. This classification definitively separates it from true vascular malformations and emphasizes its acquired, proliferative nature rather than a congenital developmental anomaly.

questions.q: A 3-month-old infant presents with a 6-day fever and only two mucocutaneous findings consistent with Kawasaki disease. Which statement best explains why this age group requires heightened clinical suspicion despite the incomplete presentation?
opts: Infants have a robust immune response that masks the full clinical syndrome
Infants younger than 6 months are at paradoxically highest risk for severe coronary artery aneurysms, and incomplete presentation often delays critical IVIg treatment
Infants develop adult-like manifestations with prominent adenopathy instead of classic features
Infants with incomplete Kawasaki disease have better coronary outcomes than those with complete disease
questions.exp: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is most commonly seen in infants younger than 6 months, who paradoxically face the highest risk for life-threatening coronary artery complications. The incomplete clinical presentation (fewer than 4 of 5 classic criteria) frequently delays diagnosis and treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), resulting in worse outcomes. Diagnosis in this age group relies on supportive laboratory findings (ESR ≥40 mm/h, CRP ≥3.0 mg/dL) or echocardiographic evidence of coronary abnormalities.
questions.🏰 Palace: Picture a tiny 3-month-old BABY in the castle nursery holding a SMALL CROWN of only 2 criteria, but a HUGE CORONARY SWORD hanging above—incomplete presentation = incomplete warning = maximum danger for the smallest patients.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with ivory-white papules and nodules (2–8 mm) coalescing into a reticular 'pebbly' pattern over his back and scapulae. He also has extensive dermal melanocytosis, generalized hirsutism, and coarse facial features. Skeletal survey shows dysostosis multiplex. Ophthalmological examination confirms clear corneas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: MPS Type I (Hurler Syndrome)
MPS Type II (Hunter Syndrome)
MPS Type III (Sanfilippo Syndrome)
Gaucher Disease Type 1
questions.exp: The pathognomonic ivory-white papules coalescing into a 'pebbly' reticular pattern on the back and scapulae, combined with X-linked inheritance affecting males, dysostosis multiplex, and crucially the ABSENCE of corneal clouding, are diagnostic of MPS Type II (Hunter Syndrome), caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency. MPS Type I presents with severe corneal clouding, which distinguishes it from Hunter syndrome.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: Picture a HUNTER (MPS II) shooting IVORY PEBBLES at the BACK of a CASTLE (no cloudy WINDOWS/corneas), while his X chromosome flag flies overhead.

questions.q: A 7-year-old girl presents with depigmented patches on the left side of her face and neck that appeared over 3 months and have remained stable. Which pathophysiological feature best explains why this presentation is characteristic of childhood vitiligo compared to adult-onset disease?
opts: Segmental vitiligo accounts for 15–30% of pediatric cases versus <5% in adults, reflecting early migration arrest of neural crest cells
Childhood vitiligo exclusively targets hair follicle melanocytes rather than basal layer melanocytes
The disease follows true dermatomal distributions in children but converts to non-dermatomal patterns in adulthood
Melanocyte destruction in children is driven by CD4+ helper T cells rather than CD8+ cytotoxic T cells
questions.exp: Segmental vitiligo (SV) is uniquely prominent in children, accounting for 15–30% of pediatric vitiligo cases compared to adult-onset disease. SV presents as unilateral, block-like, or band-shaped distributions following Blaschkoid patterns, and typically remains stable after the initial rapid progression phase. Vitiligo always targets the basal layer and hair follicle bulge melanocytes in both children and adults; the pathogenic cascade is driven by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and IFN-γ/CXCL10 signaling in both age groups.

questions.q: Why is the term 'pyogenic granuloma' considered a double misnomer?
opts: It is caused by pyogenic bacteria and contains true granulomatous inflammation
It is neither pyogenic in origin nor a true granuloma histologically, and is actually a reactive vascular hyperplasia
It produces purulent exudate but lacks epithelioid histiocytes
It is bacterial in aetiology but contains only capillary endothelial cells
questions.exp: The lesion is not driven by bacterial infection (not pyogenic) and lacks granulomatous architecture with multinucleated giant cells and epithelioid histiocytes (not a true granuloma). Instead, it represents a reactive vascular hyperplasia mimicking exuberantly proliferating granulation tissue.

questions.q: A 2-day-old infant born via vaginal delivery presents with multiple grouped vesicles on the scalp and perioral region, along with chorioretinitis and microcephaly noted on imaging. The mother had primary genital HSV infection diagnosed at 32 weeks of gestation. What is the estimated mortality risk for this presentation if left untreated?
opts: 0% mortality; SEM disease has benign prognosis
Approximately 100% mortality; congenital intrauterine infection with multisystem involvement
5–10% mortality; limited to cutaneous disease
25% risk of spontaneous abortion only; no neonatal mortality
questions.exp: The constellation of cutaneous lesions present at birth within 48 hours, combined with chorioretinitis and microcephaly, indicates congenital intrauterine HSV infection rather than perinatal SEM disease. True intrauterine HSV transmission results in devastating multisystem disease with untreated mortality approaching 100% and approximately 70% of affected infants displaying active herpetic vesicles at delivery.

questions.q: A 2-week-old neonate presents with severe generalized erythroderma, fine diffuse scaling, and profound barrier dysfunction leading to hypernatremic dehydration and failure to thrive. Genetic testing reveals biallelic mutations in the SPINK5 gene on chromosome 5q32. Which protein deficiency directly results in uncontrolled activation of serine proteases and corneodesmome degradation in this condition?
opts: Filaggrin (FLG)
LEKTI (lympho-epithelial Kazal-type related inhibitor)
Transglutaminase 1 (TGM1)
Claudin-1 (CLDN1)
questions.exp: Netherton syndrome results from biallelic SPINK5 gene mutations encoding LEKTI, a serine protease inhibitor normally localized to the spinous and granular layers. Loss of LEKTI removes physiological inhibition of kallikreins 5 and 7 and elastase 2, leading to premature corneodesmome degradation and catastrophic barrier failure. This distinguishes Netherton from other ichthyoses caused by filaggrin or transglutaminase mutations.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a NETHERTON KNIGHT standing guard at the SPINOUS GATE with a LEKTI LOCK—when the lock breaks, wild SERINE PROTEASE WOLVES devour the CORNEODESMOME BRICKS of the castle wall, leaving it in erythrodermic RUINS.

questions.q: A 6-month-old with recessive dystrophic EB presents with multiple blistered wounds and a clinical suspicion of Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization based on purulent drainage. The parents ask whether continuous topical antibiotic ointment or daily oral antibiotics should be started immediately. According to EB wound care principles, what is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Start broad-spectrum oral antibiotics immediately to prevent systemic sepsis, the leading cause of mortality in severe EB
Apply topical antibiotic ointments twice daily to all wounds to sterilize the skin surface

Perform routine bathing or soaking in dilute sodium hypochlorite (~0.005%) or 0.25% acetic acid baths to reduce bacterial colonization, reserving systemic antibiotics for culture-proven clinical infections
Apply traditional adhesive-backed antimicrobial dressings to provide continuous antibiotic delivery while minimizing dressing changes
questions.exp: EB supportive care prioritizes preventing antibiotic resistance by avoiding chronic topical or oral antibiotic use. Dilute hypochlorite or acetic acid soaks safely reduce bacterial colonization without inducing resistance. Systemic antibiotics are reserved for documented, cultured clinical infections—not empirical colonization. Traditional adhesive dressings are absolutely contraindicated in EB due to risk of iatrogenic trauma.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 9] supportive care principles, EB Nurse role

questions.q: A 3-month-old boy is diagnosed with aplasia cutis congenita of the scalp associated with short digits, syndactyly, and cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita. Genetic testing reveals an autosomal dominant mutation in ARHGAP31. Which of the following best describes the pathogenic mechanism underlying this disorder?
opts: HLA-associated autoimmune destruction of keratinocytes and hair follicles
Intrauterine vascular ischemia and placental infarctions causing tissue disruption during rapid embryonic brain growth
Immune complex deposition and antibody-mediated epidermal-dermal separation
Abnormal vascular regulation and limb development resulting from defects in morphogenic signaling pathways
questions.exp: Adams-Oliver syndrome (scalp ACC with limb reduction abnormalities) arises from mutations in vascular and developmental genes like ARHGAP31, RBPJ, NOTCH1, and DLL4, leading to defects in vascular regulation and embryonic morphogenesis rather than autoimmune mechanisms. Aplasia cutis congenita is a structural developmental disorder caused by genetic mutations, teratogens, vascular events, or intrauterine trauma—not immune-mediated, with no HLA associations.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine ARHGAP31 as an ARCHITECT building BLOOD VESSEL ROADS and LIMB BRIDGES in the castle, but the blueprints are TORN—creating missing DIGITS and SCARRED PATHWAYS instead of smooth vasculature.

questions.q: A 6-year-old girl with Naegeli-Franceschetti-Jadassohn syndrome is brought to the dermatology clinic. Her mother reports that the striking reticulate hyperpigmentation that was prominent on the neck and axillae during early childhood now appears to be gradually fading. Which additional clinical finding would you expect to elicit on examination?
opts: Well-developed, symmetric dermatoglyphics on palms and soles
Profuse palmoplantar hyperhidrosis with normal heat tolerance
Complete absence of dermatoglyphics (fingerprints and friction ridges) on palms and soles
Progressive darkening and intensification of reticulate pigmentation with age
questions.exp: Naegeli-Franceschetti-Jadassohn syndrome is pathognomonic for complete absence of dermatoglyphics (fingerprints and friction ridges), which persist throughout life despite the gradual fading of reticulate hyperpigmentation during adolescence. This is a permanent ectodermal dysplasia feature caused by disrupted keratin 14 structure affecting basal layer keratinocytes during friction ridge formation.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a FINGERPRINT SCANNER at the castle gate that NEVER activates—NO RIDGES EVER—but the PURPLE NET CLOAK (reticulate pigmentation) around the knight's shoulders FADES as she ages, yet her BLANK FINGERLESS HANDS remain FOREVER SMOOTH and UNIDENTIFIABLE.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with a light-brown patch on the trunk with superimposed dark, completely flat speckles arranged in a uniform polka-dot pattern. Histopathology shows lentiginous melanocytic hyperplasia in the basal layer with dark speckles confined to the dermal-epidermal junction at the tips of rete ridges. Which variant of naevus spilus does this represent?
opts: Naevus spilus papulosus
Naevus spilus maculosus
Naevus spilus-type congenital melanocytic nevus
Phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica
questions.exp: The clinical description of a uniform polka-dot pattern with completely flat (macular) speckles, combined with histopathology showing epidermal and junctional involvement only, is characteristic of naevus spilus maculosus. The papulosus variant features raised speckles with dermal extension and a haphazard star-map pattern.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: Picture FLAT POLKA DOTS (maculosus) dancing across a café-au-lait BALLROOM FLOOR at the dermal-epidermal JUNCTION—completely level with the dance floor, no bumps allowed!

questions.q: A 7-year-old girl with severe coarse facial features ('gargoylism'), profound generalized hypertrichosis, and extensive dermal melanocytosis is found on slit-lamp examination to have bilateral corneal clouding. Genetic testing reveals mutations in the *IDUA* gene. Which statement best describes the enzymatic defect and inheritance pattern?
opts: Deficiency of iduronate-2-sulfatase; X-linked recessive inheritance
Deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase; autosomal recessive inheritance
Deficiency of galactocerebrosidase; autosomal recessive inheritance
Deficiency of sphingomyelinase; autosomal dominant inheritance
questions.exp: MPS Type I (Hurler Syndrome) is caused by mutations in the *IDUA* gene encoding alpha-L-iduronidase, leading to glycosaminoglycan accumulation. It follows autosomal recessive inheritance and is distinguished from MPS Type II by the presence of corneal clouding and the absence of the pathognomonic 'pebbly' ivory papules. The severe phenotype (Hurler) exhibits profound coarse facies and hypertrichosis.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: HURLER (MPS I) girls are AUTOSOMAL (both X and Y gates open) and CLOUDY-EYED (corneal clouding), not the PEBBLY-BACKED HUNTER boys with clear eyes.

questions.q: A 10-day-old neonate presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the left scalp, corresponding to the fetal scalp electrode placement site during delivery. The mother is asymptomatic with no known history of genital herpes. Which of the following best describes the most likely transmission risk scenario and classification of this infection?
opts: Primary maternal infection in the third trimester with 30–50% transmission risk; perinatal SEM disease
Recurrent maternal genital herpes with <1–3% transmission risk; congenital intrauterine disease
Asymptomatic maternal shedding with transmission during vaginal delivery; perinatal SEM disease
Postpartum acquisition from environmental contamination; postnatal disseminated disease
questions.exp: The presentation at day 10 with localized vesicles at the scalp electrode site is classic for perinatal SEM disease acquired during passage through an infected birth canal. Critically, 70–90% of neonates with HSV infection are born to asymptomatic mothers with no known history of genital herpes, making this the most likely scenario despite the mother's lack of symptoms.

questions.q: Regarding the pathogenesis of Kawasaki disease, which of the following best describes why it is NOT classified as a primary autoimmune disease despite being a systemic vasculitis?
opts: Kawasaki disease targets specific desmoglein adhesion molecules, similar to pemphigus vulgaris
The causative agent is a known bacterial toxin that cleaves specific host tissue proteins
No specific host autoantigen has been identified; pathogenesis involves an aberrant immune hyper-reaction to an unidentified infectious agent in genetically susceptible individuals
Kawasaki disease exclusively affects the epidermis rather than deeper vascular structures
questions.exp: Kawasaki disease is a systemic medium-sized muscular artery vasculitis triggered by an unidentified infectious agent (likely a respiratory virus or superantigen) in a genetically susceptible host, but no specific host autoantigen or receptor has been identified. Although IgA antibodies from KD patients bind to intracellular cytoplasmic inclusions in respiratory epithelium (suggesting an intracellular viral pathogen), the disease mechanism is driven by aberrant immune activation rather than autoantibody-mediated tissue destruction. The vascular damage occurs through neutrophilic necrotizing arteritis, CD8+ T-cell infiltration, and myofibroblastic proliferation—not through specific autoantigen targeting.
questions.🏰 Palace: Imagine a CASTLE GATE labeled 'AUTOIMMUNE' with a LOCK (specific antigen), but the Kawasaki INTRUDER sneaks in through the MOAT (unknown virus), triggering the entire KINGDOM (immune system) to overreact wildly—no lock required, just chaos.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate presents with a 3 cm × 2 cm dark brown, slightly elevated lesion on the left shoulder. Clinical examination reveals coarse terminal hair overlying a rugose surface. Which genetic mutation is most likely responsible for this congenital melanocytic nevus?
opts: BRAF V600E mutation
NRAS mutation at codon 61
TP53 germline mutation
PTEN loss-of-function mutation
questions.exp: NRAS mutations at codon 61 are detected in approximately 70–80% of congenital melanocytic nevi and are highly associated with larger lesions and satellite nevi. This 3 cm lesion with hypertrichosis and rugose surface represents a medium CMN (1.5–20 cm projected adult size), a category strongly linked to NRAS mutations in the MAPK signaling cascade.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with progressive reticulate hyperpigmentation on the neck and axillae, complete absence of fingerprints on palms and soles, and severe heat intolerance. His father has identical features. Genetic testing reveals a nonsense mutation in the KRT14 gene on chromosome 17q11.2-q21. Which statement correctly describes the pathophysiological mechanism underlying this condition?
opts: Autoimmune-mediated keratinocyte destruction triggered by pathogenic anti-desmoglein antibodies
Structural and functional defect in epidermal keratinocytes leading to increased susceptibility to pro-apoptotic stimuli
HLA-associated T-cell mediated immune response against basal layer antigens
Immune-complex deposition within the basement membrane zone causing epidermal-dermal separation
questions.exp: Naegeli-Franceschetti-Jadassohn syndrome is an autosomal dominant ectodermal dysplasia caused by KRT14 mutations, which impairs keratinocyte structural integrity rather than triggering autoimmunity. The nonsense mutation results in keratinocytes that are highly susceptible to pro-apoptotic signals, not antibody-mediated destruction. This is fundamentally NOT an autoimmune or immunobullous disease.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a KERATIN CASTLE made of WOBBLY BLOCKS (KRT14 mutation) that CRUMBLE when touched—NOT attacked by ARMORED KNIGHTS (antibodies)—the blocks themselves are WEAK, so they undergo APOPTOTIC COLLAPSE.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate is suspected of having severe generalized epidermolysis bullosa (EB). The pediatric team plans to transfer the infant to a tertiary center 30 km away for specialized assessment and genetic testing. According to EB supportive care principles, what is the primary concern with standard neonatal transfer protocols in this case?
opts: The neonate will develop life-threatening sepsis during transport due to loss of skin barrier function

Mechanical trauma from standard handling and transportation may cause iatrogenic blistering and skin stripping, which should be prevented by assessment at the birthing unit by an EB clinical nurse specialist
The neonate requires immediate systemic antibiotic prophylaxis before transport to prevent bacterial colonization
Genetic testing cannot be performed unless the child is at a tertiary center, delaying diagnosis by 48 hours
questions.exp: Neonatal skin in EB is extraordinarily sensitive to mechanical trauma, and unnecessary transportation to other facilities risks iatrogenic skin stripping. EB clinical nurse specialists should ideally perform the initial assessment directly at the birthing unit to prevent preventable trauma. While infection risk exists in EB, the immediate concern during neonatal assessment and transport is avoiding mechanical injury through proper specialist handling.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 9] supportive care principles, EB Nurse role

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with postnatal growth deficiency, progressive neurological dysfunction, basal ganglia calcification, sensorineural deafness, and a characteristic 'bird-headed' facies with enophthalmia and a beaked nose. His parents report extreme photosensitivity since infancy. Genetic testing reveals an ERCC6 gene mutation. Which of the following best explains why this patient has NOT developed skin cancers despite severe UV sensitivity?
opts: Enhanced melanin production protects against UV-induced mutations
Cells with low-level DNA damage from defective TC-NER undergo apoptosis rather than accumulating carcinogenic mutations
The ERCC6 mutation activates alternative DNA repair pathways that prevent cancer development
Increased expression of tumor suppressor genes compensates for the DNA repair defect
questions.exp: Cockayne Syndrome Type I is characterized by a paradoxical cancer-sparing phenotype: despite extreme UV sensitivity and defective transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair (TC-NER), patients do not develop increased skin cancers because damaged cells undergo apoptosis rather than accumulating mutations. This protective mechanism occurs at the cost of accelerated aging and premature death.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with multiple circular patches of fine scaling and partial hair loss on the scalp. The shed hairs appear dull and gray. Wood's lamp examination shows bright green fluorescence. Trichoscopy reveals horizontal white bands on the hair shafts resembling Morse code. Which layer of the hair follicle is primarily affected in this type of tinea capitis?
opts: Internal hair shaft cortex with intact external cuticle
Scalp stratum corneum and follicle down to Adamson's fringe with arthroconidia outside the hair shaft
Deep dermal layer with granulomatous inflammation
Hair matrix with melanin disruption
questions.exp: This clinical presentation of gray patch tinea capitis with Wood's lamp fluorescence and Morse code-like hairs is pathognomonic for ectothrix variant. In ectothrix infection, fungal hyphae proliferate on the scalp surface and descend strictly to Adamson's fringe, with arthroconidia forming outside the hair shaft, which explains the external dull gray appearance from arthrospore coating.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Imagine ADAMSON's FRINGE as a castle DRAWBRIDGE—the fungus marches DOWN from the surface but STOPS exactly at the bridge (Adamson's fringe), lining the OUTSIDE of the hair shaft like soldiers on castle walls, creating GRAY MORSE CODE patterns.
